question: In the bisected angle technique, how is the X-ray beam aimed?
options: Parallel to the long axis of the tooth
Perpendicular to the long axis of the receptor
Parallel to the imaginary bisecting line
Perpendicular to the bisecting line
explanation: The beam is aimed perpendicular to an imaginary line which bisects the angle between the long axes of the image receptor and the tooth.
extraWrong: Perpendicular to the long axis of the tooth
Parallel to the long axis of the receptor

question: In the bisected angle technique, the imaginary bisecting line cuts which angle in half?
options: The angle between the receptor and the tooth
The angle between the occlusal plane and floor
The angle between the tooth and the X-ray beam
The angle between the receptor and occlusal plane
explanation: The line bisects the angle between the long axis of the image receptor and the long axis of the tooth.
extraWrong: The angle between the beam and the receptor
The angle between the palate and the floor
The angle between two adjacent teeth

question: When is the bisected angle technique needed for periapical radiography?
options: When the patient has a square or narrow dental arch
When the receptor cannot be parallel to the tooth
When only premolar and molar crowns are needed
When a long focus-to-skin distance is used
explanation: In some cases the receptor cannot be placed parallel to the tooth, so the bisected angle technique is used to prevent geometrical distortion.
extraWrong: When periodontal bone levels must be clear
When approximal caries must be detected

question: With the bisected angle technique, what does incorrect vertical angulation cause?
options: Overlapping of crowns and roots
Coning off at the edge of the anterior receptor
Elongation or foreshortening of the image
Zygomatic shadow over the molar roots
explanation: Incorrect vertical angulation results in elongation or foreshortening of the image.
extraWrong: Poor contrast between enamel and dentine

question: With the bisected angle technique, what does incorrect horizontal angulation cause?
options: Overlapping of crowns and roots
Elongation of the whole image
Foreshortening of the buccal roots
Poorly shown periodontal bone
explanation: Incorrect horizontal angulation results in overlapping of crowns and roots.

question: On bisected angle periapicals of the upper molars, the shadow of which structure is superimposed over the roots?
options: The hard palate
The nasal septum
The mandibular ramus
The zygomatic bone
explanation: The shadow of the zygomatic bone is superimposed over the roots of the upper molars, and the buccal roots are foreshortened.

question: Distortion of the crowns on bisected angle periapicals prevents the detection of what?
options: Approximal caries
Apical infection
Root fractures after trauma
Failed implants
explanation: The crowns are distorted, which prevents detection of approximal caries.

question: Which of these is an advantage of the bisected angle technique?
options: Images are reproducible
Positioning is relatively simple
Periodontal bone levels are well shown
Coning off is avoided
explanation: Positioning is relatively simple and the technique is reasonably comfortable; the other options are not true of this technique.

question: If all angulations are correctly assessed in the bisected angle technique, how good should the image be?
options: Ideal for all diagnostic purposes
Geometrically accurate with no distortion
Adequate but not ideal for most diagnosis
Unsuitable for any diagnostic purpose
explanation: If all angulations are correctly assessed, the image should be adequate, but not ideal, for most diagnostic purposes.

question: For a bisected angle periapical of posterior teeth, which receptor is used and how is it orientated?
options: Small receptor, long axis vertical
Small receptor, long axis horizontal
Large receptor, long axis vertical
Large receptor, long axis horizontal
explanation: For posterior teeth, a large phosphor plate or film packet is inserted with its long axis horizontal.
extraWrong: Two small receptors side by side

question: Coning off (cone cutting) is common with the bisected angle technique.
explanation: Coning off or cone cutting is listed as a common problem with the bisected angle technique.

question: The bisected angle technique produces reproducible images.
explanation: Reproducible images are not possible with the bisected angle technique.

question: With the bisected angle technique, the buccal roots of the upper molars appear elongated.
explanation: The buccal roots of the upper molars are foreshortened, and the zygomatic shadow overlies the roots.

question: With the bisected angle technique, both the horizontal and vertical angles have to be assessed.
explanation: Both angles have to be assessed, and this is one of the variables that can cause a distorted image.

question: Which of these is a clinical indication for periapical radiography?
options: Before, during and after endodontics
Imaging the whole skull from the side
Imaging both jaws and the TMJs on one image
Imaging only the crowns of the posterior teeth
explanation: Indications include detecting apical infection, assessing periodontal status, after trauma, assessing roots before extractions, before, during and after endodontics, before and after apical surgery, and evaluating implants.

question: For a bisected angle periapical of anterior teeth, which receptor is used and how is it orientated?
options: Small receptor, long axis horizontal
Large receptor, long axis horizontal
Small or large receptor, long axis vertical
Two receptors side by side, horizontal
explanation: For anterior teeth, a small or large intra-oral phosphor plate or film packet is inserted with its long axis vertical.

question: Why do bisected angle periapicals frequently produce distorted images?
options: A long focus-to-skin distance is used
The receptor is parallel to the tooth
The beam aiming device fixes the tubehead
There are many variables in the technique
explanation: The many variables in the bisected angle technique can frequently result in a distorted image, and both the horizontal and vertical angles have to be assessed.
extraWrong: The receptor is held firmly by a holder
The exposure time is too short
The voxel size is too large

question: The bisected angle technique is reasonably comfortable for the patient.
explanation: Being reasonably comfortable is one of the advantages of the bisected angle technique, along with relatively simple positioning.

question: Bisected angle technique periapical radiographs involve positioning the x-ray tubehead so the main beam meets the image receptor at right angles?
explanation: Don't want right angles. The beam should meet the bisecting line at right angles (imaginary line between the image receptor & tooth).

question: When taking a bisected angle technique periapical, at what angle should the main beam hit the image receptor?
options: Main beam should be parallel to the image receptor
Position tubehead so main beam hits image receptor at right angles
Image receptor is perpendicular to main beam
Angle depends on alignment of image receptor & tooth
explanation: Don't want right angles, different for each patient.

question: An advantage of the bisected angle technique is that it is possible to obtain reproducible views?
explanation: Position of image receptor & tubehead are estimated by eye - impossible to make exact reproductions.
